title: Nepal has two decades to turn its youth bulge into an economic dividend, World Bank reports - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal has two decades to turn its youth bulge into an economic dividend, World Bank reports  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal has over two decades to capitalise on its expanding working-age population before the demographic advantage begins to fade. However, according to a new World Bank report, structural weaknesses in employment, healthcare and social protection could prevent the country from translating this opportunity into sustained economic growth.

Nepal's working-age population is projected to peak in 2047, giving it a longer window than most South Asian countries to benefit from what economists call the demographic dividend—the potential economic gains that arise when the share of the working-age population increases relative to dependents.

The country is expected to become an aged society by 2059, when the share of older people will rise significantly, according to the World Bank report—Demographic Change in South Asia: From Tailwinds to Headwinds for Development—released on Tuesday.

The report warns that South Asia's demographic advantage is gradually disappearing, with the region's working-age population of 1.17 billion expected to peak in less than a decade and begin shrinking.

By 2049, South Asia will become an aged region, with 14 percent of its population aged 65 and above.

The transition is happening faster and at a lower level of per capita income than in comparable emerging and developing economies, leaving countries with less time to create productive jobs and establish systems to support ageing populations.

While Nepal has more time than its neighbours, the country's ability to benefit from its demographic transition remains constrained by a narrow employment base, persistent gender inequalities, weak healthcare infrastructure and inadequate retirement protection.

Remittances compare to a quarter of Nepal's gross domestic product. Money sent home by Nepalis working abroad contributed to 40 percent of poverty reduction between 2001 and 2011. But the economic gains from overseas employment have not necessarily translated into higher productivity at home.

Returnee migrant workers earn lower salaries than non-migrants for approximately three years after returning, suggesting that skills and experience acquired abroad do not easily find productive employment in the domestic economy, the report says.

The findings highlight the need to connect vocational training with job placement and life-skills programmes to improve the employment prospects of returnee migrants.

Nepal also faces significant barriers to increasing women's participation in the economy. Women work, on average, nine hours less per week than men. This largely reflects unequal care responsibilities that limit women’s ability to participate in paid employment.

Adolescent fertility rates also remain high, affecting girls' educational attainment and future employment opportunities.

Healthcare access is another major constraint. Around 60 percent of doctors in Nepal are based in urban areas, despite the predominantly rural distribution of the population. The readiness of health facilities to provide services for noncommunicable diseases stands at just 28.4 percent.

These shortcomings could become more costly as the population ages and demand for long-term healthcare increases.

The employment structure presents another challenge. Although construction companies have recorded strong employment growth, largely driven by hydropower development, the overall employment base remains narrow.

The report says the country needs to create more productive jobs, strengthen private sector participation, improve access to finance for micro, small and medium enterprises, and invest in education, skills and healthcare to maximise its demographic advantage.

The challenge is not limited to creating jobs for young people. Nepal must also prepare for a rapidly growing elderly population, most of whom currently lack adequate income security, the report said.

Approximately 91 percent of Nepali workers aged 65 and above are employed in the informal sector, leaving the overwhelming majority outside contributory pension arrangements.

Nepal's Social Security Fund, established in 2018, provides a foundation for expanding social insurance coverage. The contributory scheme is financed through a 31 percent contribution rate, with the government providing matching contributions of 9 percent for informal workers.

The World Bank says scaling up such arrangements could significantly expand old-age income security.

The government also provides a universal Senior Citizen's Allowance of Rs4,000 per month to citizens aged 70 and above, and those aged 60 and above in the Dalit community and Karnali region.

The report says this non-contributory pension provides a critical income floor that should be preserved and progressively expanded.

The demographic challenge is regional, but Nepal's relatively longer preparation period offers an opportunity to build institutions and policies before the pressure of population ageing intensifies.

South Asia's demographic transition has already contributed significantly to economic expansion. Since 2000, a growing share of adults in their prime working years has helped increase the region's annual GDP growth by 0.4 percentage points and labour productivity by 1.1 percentage points.

But that contribution is expected to decline sharply. The annual contribution of demographic changes to regional GDP growth is projected to fall to just 0.1 percentage point between now and 2050.

Only 60 percent of South Asia's working-age population is employed, while 88 percent of those with jobs work informally, often with lower earnings and limited job security.

The region also has one of the world's weakest pension systems. Only 17 percent of its working-age population contributes to a pension scheme, while just 10 percent of older people receive pension benefits—the lowest coverage globally.

"South Asian economies are ageing faster and earlier in their development journeys," said Johannes Zutt, World Bank vice-president for South Asia.

"They need to act now to adopt policies and build infrastructure that create more and better jobs and deepen the gains from their 'youth dividend', while at the same time preparing for ageing," he said.

full_article:
An Indian tourist was killed and a New Zealand tourist injured when two helicopters collided while preparing to land near Mount Everest in Nepal on November 3, Reuters reported, citing local authorities and airline officials.

The collision occurred in the Everest base camp area, according to Kaman Singh Thapa Magar, the chief district officer of Solukhumbu district. The injured New Zealander was rescued.

The helicopters belonged to two private Nepalese operators, Fishtail Air and Dynasty Air.

Fishtail Air said its helicopter was carrying tourists who had been evacuated from the Everest region when the accident occurred during landing. Dynasty Air said its helicopter was transporting cargo only.

The collision took place during Nepal's peak trekking season, when helicopters regularly transport hikers and climbers in the Everest region.

title: Nepal to strongly raise climate justice and mountain conservation issues at COP31: Minister Chaudhary - Khabarhub
description: Nepal to strongly raise climate justice and mountain conservation issues at COP31: Minister Chaudhary  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Minister for Agriculture, Forest and Environment Gita Chaudhary has said Nepal will strongly raise issues of climate justice, adequate climate financing and mountain conservation at the upcoming 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31).

Speaking at a programme organised by Friedrich Ebert Stiftung Nepal in Kathmandu on Tuesday, Minister Chaudhary said that although Nepal’s contribution to the global climate crisis was negligible, its people were bearing the consequences of a crisis they had not created.

She said Nepal had received USD 21.6 million from the Loss and Damage Fund, while approval had been granted to submit three projects worth around USD 45 million to the Adaptation Fund.

Minister Chaudhary stressed that adequate climate financing should be provided on time in the form of grants rather than loans.

She also highlighted that Nepal, in collaboration with Bhutan, had proposed including the issue of 1.5°C warming in mountain regions on the COP31 agenda.

The minister called on developed countries to fulfil their climate financing commitments, triple support for adaptation measures and give priority to the concerns of mountain communities in global climate discussions.

She further expressed the government’s commitment to ensuring the participation of women, Indigenous nationalities, Dalits and youths in climate-related initiatives and extending climate finance to the local level.

full_article:

Grass Roots: How ban came about

Fifty years after Nepal banned all cannabis cultivation, Supreme Court has directed govt to frame regulations within three months to allow its controlled cultivation for medicinal, scientific and industrial purposes, potentially opening the door to a legal cannabis industry in the Himalayan nation. The court held that successive govts had failed to implement provisions of a law enacted in 1976 that already allowed limited cultivation under regulation.The verdict, delivered on May 18, 2025, remained unpublished for nearly 18 months after court records were destroyed in an arson attack during the violent Gen Z protests on Sept 9, 2025. Its full text emerged only last week, bringing renewed attention to a ban Nepal imposed in 1976 under international pressure, particularly from the US.The court criticised successive govts for failing to implement provisions of the Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act, 1976, which permits certain forms of regulated cultivation and medicinal use. "The failure to do so amounts to a refusal or neglect by govt to discharge its legal obligations," the court observed. It directed authorities to frame rules for licensing and monitoring the cultivation, processing, storage, sale, distribution, import and export of cannabis within three months of receiving the order."It is therefore the duty of state authorities to formulate such rules without delay," the judgment said in a published English translation. The order did not permit recreational use, which remains illegal, and left any wider relaxation of cannabis laws to parliament.The ruling could bring new opportunities for farmers in Nepal's mountainous regions, where cannabis grows naturally and cultivation has continued illegally despite the ban. Campaigners have argued for years that prohibition did little to stop production while denying farmers a source of income. They believe a regulated industry could give growers access to legal markets and create jobs in processing, medicine and other cannabis-based products.Rajiv Kafle, a prominent cannabis legalisation campaigner, has long called for Nepal to replace prohibition with regulation. "In fact, regulation is a better policy option," he told, pointing to the economic opportunities that countries with legal cannabis industries had already begun exploiting.Former health minister Birodh Khatiwada, another advocate of legalisation, has questioned why Nepal continued to criminalise a crop that several other countries had begun permitting. "It is not justifiable that a poor country like ours has to treat cannabis as a drug," he said earlier, criticising the difference between restrictions in developing countries and changing policies in wealthier nations.Saurav Dhakal of Green Growth Nepal has also argued that cannabis cultivation could help rural communities, but warned that large companies should not be allowed to corner the benefits. "We need to make sure that legalising cannabis benefits the neediest Nepalis," he said, calling for small farmers and cooperatives to have a meaningful share in any future legal industry.Nepal has made several attempts to ease its cannabis restrictions, but little has changed on the ground. A parliamentary Bill introduced in 2020 failed to make progress, while a 2024 govt announcement allowing medicinal cannabis cultivation produced few results. Gandaki Province passed legislation in July 2026 permitting regulated cultivation for medicinal and industrial purposes, but federal restrictions continued to complicate its implementation.During the 1960s and early 1970s, Kathmandu's Freak Street became a prominent stop on the hippie trail, attracting Western backpackers, counterculture travellers and Americans seeking to avoid conscription during the Vietnam War. Govt-licensed shops openly sold marijuana and hashish. As then US President Richard Nixon intensified the 'War on Drugs', Nepal faced mounting pressure to shut down the trade.In 1973, Nepal revoked cannabis trading licences, closing the licensed hashish shops. The Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act, 1976, subsequently criminalised cultivation, sale and consumption, although it retained limited exceptions for regulated activities that successive govts failed to implement.Ironically, several US states have legalised recreational marijuana years ago, while Nepal continues to criminalise unauthorised cultivation and consumption.

title: Indian Held in Nepal for Possession of Firecrackers - Deccan Chronicle
description: Indian Held in Nepal for Possession of Firecrackers  Deccan Chronicle
publisher.title: Deccan Chronicle
full_article:
Kathmandu: Nepal Police have arrested an Indian national from Kathmandu on charges of possessing firecrackers, which are banned in the Himalayan country, ahead of the festival of Diwali.

Raman Kumar Mehta, 29, from Motihari in Bihar, was arrested from Tinchule in the eastern part of Kathmandu on Tuesday along with a huge quantity of firecrackers, police said.

Police confiscated various types of firecrackers amounting to NPR 400,000 from him. The firecrackers were recovered from his rented room at Tinchule-Bouddha during a raid.

The government has banned the sale, purchase and use of firecrackers within the country citing security reasons.

Despite being declared illegal, people especially youths secretly acquire firecrackers from markets in Kathmandu and burn them during Diwali festival.

Firecrackers are brought mainly from India through illegal channels. The government has declared a holiday for five days during Diwali also known as Tihar, starting from November 8.

The five-day festival starts on Sunday, with Kukur Tihar, when dogs are fed and worshipped and ends with Bhai Tika, when sisters worship brothers wishing for their long life, good health and prosperity.

This year Laxmi Puja and Kukuar Tihar lie on the same day, Sunday, as the festival is celebrated on the basis of Lunar calendar.

title: Nepal fines six Indian trekkers rescued from remote Dolpa - Everest Chronicle
description: Nepal fines six Indian trekkers rescued from remote Dolpa  Everest Chronicle
publisher.title: Everest Chronicle
full_article:
Six Indian trekkers who trekked into Nepal's remote Upper Dolpa region without permits or a guide and ignored weather warnings have been fined after being rescued by helicopter, officials said.

The six were rescued on Monday from the Numala-Bungla pass, at an altitude of around 4,500 metres, in Shey Phoksundo Rural Municipality-8 after becoming stranded in heavy snowfall.

They had no telephone network or other means of communication, but a porter travelling with the group managed to descend to a nearby village and alert local authorities.

The government spent around one million rupees ($6,600) on the helicopter rescue, which involved two shuttle flights from the pass to the district headquarters of Dunai, following an initial flight from Pokhara, officials said.

"Fortunately, they had found a safe place and were in good health," Dolpa Chief District Officer Junu Hamal Dhakal said.

The trekkers were identified as Momita Haldar, Piyali Kole, Jajala Trived Kumar, Aditya Singh, Dipalina Biswas and Rajesh D.

Officials said the group had deliberately taken alternative routes to avoid checkpoints operated by national park authorities and the local administration to enter the restricted area.

The district administration had instructed security agencies weeks earlier to prevent trekkers from entering high-altitude areas ahead of Cyclone Arnab, which brought heavy rainfall to Nepal from October 28 to 30.

The administration had also issued warnings about possible snowfall and hazardous conditions in Upper Dolpa. The six lost contact on October 31 after becoming stranded in the snow.

Under Nepal's regulations, foreigners entering Upper Dolpa without the required permit face a fine of 50,000 rupees. However, authorities reduced the penalty, citing the trekkers' limited knowledge of the remote terrain and local regulations.

Each trekker was fined at least 20,000 rupees for violating regulations and charged a permit fee of $40 for staying nearly two weeks in Upper Dolpa without notifying local authorities, bringing the total amount paid by the group to 160,000 rupees, Dhakal said.

Foreign visitors are charged $20 for a seven-day permit, with an additional $5 for each subsequent day.

The trekkers had travelled without permits and did not have travel insurance, officials said, adding that the absence of insurance made the rescue operation more complicated.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority coordinated the helicopter evacuation, which cost around one million rupees.

Upper Dolpa is among Nepal's most remote trekking destinations, where difficult terrain, limited communications and rapidly changing weather can make rescue operations challenging.

The district administration has urged trekkers to obtain the necessary permits, follow official weather warnings and make appropriate arrangements before travelling to high-altitude areas.

Two helicopters have collided while attempting to land in Nepal's Mount Everest region, killing an Indian tourist and injuring two other people, according to initial reports. The accident happened on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, near Pheriche village, below Mount Everest's South Base Camp, during one of Nepal's busiest trekking periods. Two private helicopter companies, Fishtail Air and Air Dynasty, operated the aircraft, which reportedly approached the same landing area when the collision occurred.

The incident has raised fresh concerns about helicopter operations in the Himalayas, where aviation plays an important role in transporting tourists, rescuing stranded trekkers, and supporting mountaineering expeditions. Although helicopters provide an essential transportation link in this remote region, operating at extreme altitudes presents considerable challenges for pilots and aircraft. Authorities are investigating the circumstances surrounding the collision.

According to ABC News, the collision occurred at Pheriche village, approximately 13,780 feet (4,200 meters) above sea level. The helicopters involved belonged to Fishtail Air and Air Dynasty, two private operators serving Nepal's mountainous regions. Fishtail Air confirmed its aircraft was transporting passengers, while an Air Dynasty representative said its helicopter was carrying cargo . The incident occurred during a particularly busy period for trekking tourism , with thousands of visitors traveling through the region after improved weather conditions.

Airbus AS350 Helicopters Were Involved In The Accident

Credit: Daz Hopper Photography | Shutterstock

Further details published by The Kathmandu Post identified both aircraft as Airbus AS350 helicopters. The Air Dynasty aircraft, registered as 9N-AOD, departed Lukla Airport on a cargo flight, while Fishtail Air's 9N-AJR took off from Gorakshep carrying two foreign nationals. The collision reportedly happened at approximately 08:12 AM local time, as the helicopters approached the helipad from opposite directions.

Footage verified by the BBC showed the helicopters' rotor blades clipping each other shortly before both aircraft came down. According to The Kathmandu Post, the collision occurred when the helicopters were still approximately 2–3 meters above the ground. The circumstances surrounding the accident remain under investigation, although preliminary reports point to a possible communication failure between the pilots .

The Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal (CAAN) is investigating the collision. Its director general, Mukesh Dangol, suggested that communication difficulties could have contributed to the incident because the location is outside the coverage of Lukla Airport's air traffic control tower. He explained that pilots operating in the area must communicate directly with one another.

Dangol told The Kathmandu Post:

“Preliminary reports suggest miscommunication between the pilots, as the area is outside the coverage of Lukla Airport's air traffic control tower and pilots have to communicate with each other”.

The latest accident adds to a history of serious helicopter incidents in the Everest region. In July 2023, a Manang Air Airbus AS350 B3e crashed in the Lamajura area of Solukhumbu district while returning to Kathmandu following a sightseeing flight. All six people aboard the helicopter died, including five Mexican tourists from the same family and the Nepali pilot, according to The Kathmandu Post.

Helicopter operations in the Everest region have also faced growing criticism from local communities concerned about noise pollution, environmental damage, and the rising number of sightseeing flights. In December 2025, local authorities and Sagarmatha National Park issued directives restricting sightseeing helicopter flights over the park, except for rescue operations. The restrictions were scheduled to take effect on January 1, 2026.

Nevertheless, helicopters remain essential to Nepal's mountain tourism industry. With no road access to many settlements and trekking locations, aircraft provide a vital means of transporting supplies, supporting climbers, and evacuating people with altitude sickness or injuries. The latest collision will likely renew discussions about air traffic coordination, landing procedures, and operational safety in one of the world's most challenging environments.

SCENE REPORT

Extreme Conditions: Inside Nepal’s Metal Underground

By J. Bennett · Illustration by Jordan Warren · November 03, 2026

Westerners might know it as the southern base of Mount Everest or the birthplace of Buddha, but—like so many places—Nepal’s recent headlines clash with the tourist brochure. Nestled between India and China, the South Asian country has endured a Gen Z political massacre, a toppled government, and devastating flash floods in just the last year. But lurking beneath the headlines, far from the mountain-climbing and the religious-pilgrimage industries, is a small but thriving underground culture that holds little interest for most visitors: Nepali extreme metal.

“The underground scene in Nepal has always stayed underground,” says Darshan Angdembe Limbu, guitarist and vocalist for the Nepali death metal band Animality. “Bands come and go because that’s just life here. A lot of musicians eventually leave Nepal for work or studies, so many bands have a short lifespan. But every time that happens, there’s always a younger generation starting new bands and carrying the scene forward. That’s why I think the underground never really dies.”

Centered in the capital of Kathmandu, Nepal’s metal scene is almost entirely DIY. “There isn’t really an industry behind extreme metal in Nepal,” Limbu says. “Most shows are organized by bands, friends, and people in the scene. Everyone knows each other, supports each other, and there’s healthy competition. The scene works because it’s already a community.”

Unlike North America or Europe, where subgenres can thrive on hyper-specific bills, Nepal’s metal scene isn’t segregated. “We don’t really have separate death metal, grindcore, thrash, or hardcore scenes,” Limbu says. “Most gigs are mixed bills, so people are exposed to all kinds of extreme music. I think that’s one reason the community feels so connected. International bands are always exciting because they’re rare, but local bands also receive a huge amount of support.”

Animality grew out of the political death metal tradition partly established by Sepultura rather than the satanic fantasia of Morbid Angel or gore-porn misogyny of Cannibal Corpse. In fact, you can draw a straight line from the socially conscious, self-proclaimed “riot music” of Sepultura’s Chaos A.D. and Animality’s 2026 album Third World Brutality (even though the Nepali band has more in common sonically with Behemoth). Just as the members of Sepultura grew up under a Brazilian military dictatorship that collapsed in 1985, the members of Animality witnessed the overthrow of the Nepali government in September of 2025.

“Our music comes from everyday observation rather than fantasy,” Limbu says. “Extreme music became the way to express things that couldn’t always be expressed in ordinary life. Third World Brutality wasn’t planned as a concept album. The songs were written over many years, and only after everything was finished did the title naturally fit the whole record. The album reflects the environment we come from and the observations that shaped it.”

As Limbu explains, most metal shows in Nepal before 2013–14 took place outside. “There wasn’t really a culture of hosting metal shows in pubs or bars back then,” he says. “Live music was more connected to melas [fairs] and mahotsavs [community festivals], so naturally most shows happened outdoors.”

During Nepal’s civil war period of 1996 to 2006, the government clamped down on public gatherings. When the country suffered a constitutional crisis in 2013–14, restrictions resumed under what Limbu describes as “safe-mode government.” “It wasn’t just the restrictions on concerts running past 8 or 9 P.M.,” he says. “The authorities were also making it increasingly difficult to organize outdoor events, even during the daytime. So, the scene gradually started moving into bars and indoor venues, where bands could continue performing.”

title: Indian national killed as two helicopters collide in Nepal - Daily Pioneer
description: Indian national killed as two helicopters collide in Nepal  Daily Pioneer
publisher.title: Daily Pioneer
full_article:
A 47-year-old Indian national was killed and another passenger injured when two helicopters collided while landing on Tuesday in Nepal’s Solukhumbu district, police said. Indian authorities are working in close coordination with Nepali officials for early repatriation of the mortal remains of the deceased, the Indian Embassy in Nepal said.

The two helicopters collided while landing at Pheriche in Ward 4 of Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality of Solukhumbu district on Tuesday, according to a Nepal Police statement.

The helicopters, operated by Fishtail Air and Air Dynasty, collided at around 8.11 am, according to the District Police Office, Solukhumbu. Both helicopters took off from Lukla Airport, the gateway to Mt Everest.

Police Inspector Mausam Tamang said the deceased was identified as Vasanth Kumar Balaramaramadu, an Indian national travelling aboard the Fishtail Air helicopter. Shailesh Krishna Patel, a 49-year-old Indian origin resident of New Zealand who was also aboard the same helicopter, was injured in the collision, Tamang said.

“The Embassy of India in Kathmandu expresses its deepest condolences on the demise of an Indian in an incident involving a collision between two helicopters in the Solukhumbu district of Nepal today,” the Indian Embassy in Nepal said.
